date.note: The Ottoman siege began in early April 1453 and the city was taken by assault on 29 May 1453 (Jumada al-Ula 857). The last Byzantine emperor, Constantine XI Palaiologos, died in the fighting. Halil Inalcik dates the installation of Gennadios Scholarios as patriarch to 6 January 1454, following the chronology of Kritovoulos; Runciman is more hesitant about the exact date. The remaining Byzantine successor states fell soon after: the Despotate of the Morea in 1460 and the Empire of Trebizond in 1461.

summary: The Fall of Constantinople was the siege and capture of the Byzantine capital by the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II on 29 May 1453, in which the last emperor, Constantine XI Palaiologos, was killed and the Byzantine Empire came to an end. Greek writers recorded it as the catastrophe of the Christian Roman empire, Ottoman writers as the conquest (fetih) that made the city the sultan's capital, and the Orthodox patriarchate was reconstituted under Ottoman rule with Gennadios Scholarios as its first patriarch.
description:
By the mid-fifteenth century the Byzantine Empire had been reduced to Constantinople, a few islands, and the Morea; Inalcik, following the Byzantine scholar George Scholarios, describes the capital before its fall as a depopulated city of ruins whose trade had passed to the Italians and to the Ottoman cities of Bursa and Edirne. In search of western help, the Byzantine delegation at the Council of Ferrara-Florence had accepted union with Rome in 1439, but the union was resisted by much of the Byzantine clergy and populace; it was solemnly proclaimed in Hagia Sophia only in December 1452, and the anti-unionist party was led by the monk Gennadios, the former George Scholarios, who had himself supported union in the 1430s (Blanchet). Doukas, who favoured the union, reports that the grand duke Loukas Notaras said, as the Ottoman army massed before the city, 'It would be better to see the turban of the Turks reigning in the center of the City than the Latin miter.' Mehmed II, who had acceded in 1451, built the fortress of Rumeli Hisarı on the Bosporus in 1452 and opened the siege in April 1453 with a large army and heavy artillery; the defenders, including Genoese and Venetian contingents under Giovanni Giustiniani, were greatly outnumbered, though the figures given for both sides vary widely across the sources and are not adopted here.

The city fell to a general assault on 29 May 1453 and Constantine XI died in the fighting; Nicolò Barbaro reports that his fate was not known, though some said he had been seen among the dead. According to Inalcik, Mehmed proclaimed the assault in the terms of Islamic law, under which a community of the People of the Book that rejected the invitation to surrender and was subdued by force ('anwatan) was conceded no rights: 'their goods are legitimate booty and they and their children are reduced to slavery', with one fifth of the movable booty due to the ruler. Inalcik, citing Runciman, states that the sultan granted three days of sack but ended it on the evening of the first day and reserved the walls and buildings to himself, and that the Ottoman and Byzantine sources agree he toured 'the looted and enslaved city' in profound sadness; Tursun Beg reports that he then declared Istanbul his throne. The Christian accounts describe the sack in their own terms. Doukas tells how crowds took refuge in Hagia Sophia, trusting a prophecy that an angel would deliver the city, until the Turks broke the gates with axes and 'each Turk caught and bound his own captive', so that 'infinite chains of captives' were led out of the church while its icons were hacked apart and its sacred vessels seized; he reads the catastrophe as divine wrath. The Venetian Barbaro, an eyewitness in the harbour, writes in his diary that those found in the streets were put to the sword from sunrise until midday, that merchants who had hidden underground were afterwards found and sold as slaves, that men of the Ottoman fleet landed by the Jewish quarter to rob the houses of the Jews, and that nuns and young women were 'vergognade e viluperade' (dishonoured and violated) and then sold at auction across the Ottoman lands. The length and conduct of the sack are among the points on which the sources differ, and the source-critical study of Philippides and Hanak examines such conflicting reports.

Hagia Sophia became the mosque of Ayasofya. Inalcik argues that Mehmed and his successors saw themselves, as holders of the throne of the Caesars, as emperors of Rome, and that the repopulation of the city was among his first concerns: Kritovoulos, as quoted by Inalcik, reports that the sultan settled his fifth share of the enslaved Greeks along the shores of the harbour with houses and a remission of taxes, and allowed those who had paid or promised their ransom to live in the city. As part of that policy he appointed Gennadios patriarch of Constantinople (dated by Inalcik to 6 January 1454); Sphrantzes gives as the reason the wish to encourage Christians who had fled to return, while Inalcik adds that Ottoman sultans presented themselves as protectors of the Orthodox Church against the Latins. Under Gennadios the Florentine union was not upheld in the capital.

The event is narrated in distinct voices. Among Greek writers, Sphrantzes, a courtier of Constantine XI, wrote as an eyewitness who was enslaved and ransomed; Doukas, in Genoese service on Lesbos, wrote a history of the Byzantine decline that blames the divisions over the union; and Kritovoulos of Imbros, who entered Mehmed's service, dedicated a history of his reign to the sultan. Barbaro's diary gives a Venetian, Latin Christian eyewitness account. In the Ottoman voice, Tursun Beg, who was in the sultan's entourage, celebrated the conquest in his Tarih-i Ebu'l-Feth (History of the Father of Conquest). A Jewish perspective appears in the Hebrew chronicle Seder Eliyahu Zuta, completed in 1523 by Elijah Capsali of Candia, whom Martin Jacobs describes as probably the first Jew to make the Ottomans the main subject of his work and whose image of Islam he calls ambivalent. In Ottoman and later Muslim memory the conquest was linked to a prophetic report, 'You shall surely conquer Constantinople; how excellent a commander will its commander be, and how excellent an army will that army be', transmitted in the Musnad of Ahmad ibn Hanbal and in al-Hakim al-Naysaburi's al-Mustadrak; al-Hakim judged its chain sound (sahih al-isnad), al-Dhahabi in his abridgement marked it sahih, and the modern editors of the Mu'assasat al-Risala editions note that the name, father's name, and lineage of its narrator 'Abd Allah ibn Bishr (al-Ghanawi or al-Khath'ami) are disputed, and with them his reliability. Mehmed received the epithet Fatih, the Conqueror, and Feridun Emecen studies how the conquest was bound up with prophetic and apocalyptic expectations on both sides. Modern historians differ in emphasis: Runciman's narrative presents the fall as the end of the Christian Roman empire and a shock to western Christendom, Philippides and Hanak subject the Greek, Latin, Slavonic, and Ottoman sources to detailed critique, and Jonathan Harris questions the picture of an unbroken war between Islam and Christendom, stressing the Byzantine elite's divided strategies toward the Ottomans and the West.
editorial_notes: This event is filed under christianity as a storage convention per ADR-0010: the polity that fell was the Byzantine (Christian Roman) empire, consistent with fall-of-baghdad-1258 being filed under islam. The home is not a claim of ownership; the event belongs equally to Ottoman and Islamic history, and the Ottoman and Islamic perspective is represented in its own voice (Tursun Beg, the hadith and its classical gradings, and the modern Turkish historians Halil Inalcik and Feridun Emecen), alongside Greek, Latin, and Jewish voices, per neutrality principles #10 and #11. NAMING: the primary label 'Fall of Constantinople' follows English academic usage and matches the stable id; it is not a judgment. The Ottoman Turkish form (Feth-i Kostantiniyye) and the modern Turkish 'İstanbul'un Fethi' are given as aliases, and the Greek 'Halosis' as the original-script name of the Greek historiographical tradition; the entry adopts no register as the measure of another. NEUTRALITY: the Greek accounts of catastrophe and divine wrath, the Latin eyewitness account, and the Ottoman account of a celebrated conquest are attributed to their authors. The enslavement of the population is stated as Inalcik gives the legal rule and the sources' testimony, and the Christian descriptions of the sack are quoted or closely paraphrased as their authors' accounts. The hadith is quoted as a report transmitted in the Musnad and the Mustadrak; its classical and modern gradings (al-Hakim, al-Dhahabi, the Risala editors' note on the disputed narrator) are recorded as attributed positions within the traditionist discipline of hadith criticism, and the entry makes no ruling on the report's authenticity or on whether 1453 fulfilled it. The remark attributed to Loukas Notaras is reported as Doukas's attribution only, and Doukas's own pro-union stance is noted because it bears on that report. Army sizes and casualty figures differ widely across the sources and none is adopted (principle #2); the duration of the sack is reported as given by each source. SOURCING (principles #8 and #9): (a) modern historians, Runciman (1965), Philippides and Hanak (2011), Harris (2010), Blanchet (2008) on Gennadios Scholarios, and Jacobs (2005) on Capsali; (b) primary texts in several voices, the Greek historians Doukas (Magoulias trans.), Sphrantzes (Philippides trans.), and Kritovoulos (Riggs trans.), the Venetian Barbaro (Cornet ed.), the Ottoman historian Tursun Beg (Inalcik and Murphey ed. and trans.), and, for the hadith, the Musnad of Ahmad ibn Hanbal and al-Hakim's al-Mustadrak with al-Dhahabi's Talkhis; (c) modern Turkish historians (the modern Muslim-scholarship lens), Inalcik (1969-70) and Emecen (2012). No encyclopedias or tertiary sources are cited. CONFIDENCE: rated high where the passages were read directly: Inalcik (open access) for the legal rule of conquest by force and enslavement (p. 232), the sack and its ending, the 'looted and enslaved city', and Tursun Beg's report (p. 233), Kritovoulos's account of the settlement of the enslaved Greeks as quoted by Inalcik (p. 235), and the appointment of Gennadios (pp. 236-237); Doukas in Magoulias's translation for the Notaras saying (XXXVII.10) and the sack of Hagia Sophia (XXXIX.17-21); Barbaro's diary in the public-domain 1856 edition for the entry of 29 May. Al-Hakim's grading, al-Dhahabi's notation, and the Risala editors' note on the narrator were read in an online transcription of the Risala edition of the Mustadrak, not in the printed volume, so that source is rated medium; the Arna'ut editors' own grading of the Musnad report (vol. 31, no. 18957) was not seen and is not stated. All other sources were verified to exist and to be on-topic through publisher pages, library catalogues, DOIs, and scholarly reviews but were not read line by line, so they are rated medium; Kritovoulos is quoted only through Inalcik. The wording of the hadith follows a standard English rendering of the Arabic.

relations.note: The union of the Latin and Greek churches defined at Florence in 1439 was proclaimed in Hagia Sophia in December 1452, months before the siege; it was opposed by the party led by Gennadios Scholarios and was not upheld in Constantinople after he became patriarch under Ottoman rule.

The Latin capture and sack of Constantinople in 1204 during the Fourth Crusade, after which the Byzantine Empire was restored in 1261, is treated by historians as part of the long weakening of the city and the empire that ended in 1453, and it shaped Byzantine attitudes toward union with Rome.
The estrangement of the Latin and Greek churches formed the background to the Byzantine search for western aid and to the dispute over the Florentine union in the city's last years.

The Orthodox patriarchate of Constantinople was reconstituted under Ottoman rule, with Gennadios Scholarios appointed by Mehmed II as the first patriarch after the conquest; according to Inalcik, the Ottoman sultans presented themselves as protectors of the Orthodox Church against the Latins.

A prophetic report transmitted in the Musnad of Ahmad ibn Hanbal (and in al-Hakim's al-Mustadrak), praising the commander and the army that would conquer Constantinople, framed the conquest in Ottoman and later Muslim memory; its classical and modern gradings are recorded as attributed positions, without a ruling on its authenticity.
Ottoman Istanbul, the city's new identity after 1453, became one of the principal centres of the Sephardic diaspora after the expulsions from Iberia in 1492 and 1497.

Compares the question, not the answer, per neutrality principle #10. Both are the capture of an imperial capital whose ruler embodied a religious polity (the Byzantine emperor, the Abbasid caliph), raising the question of what became of each tradition's central religious-political institution when the capital fell. The difference: in 1258 the conquerors were then non-Muslim Mongols and the caliphate continued as a line of Abbasid caliphs installed in Cairo by the Mamluks, while in 1453 the Muslim conqueror made the city his own capital, the Byzantine imperial office ended, and the Orthodox patriarchate was reconstituted under his authority. This link ranks neither tradition and treats neither as the measure of the other; the framing is the editor's.

sources.citation: Inalcik, Halil. 'The Policy of Mehmed II toward the Greek Population of Istanbul and the Byzantine Buildings of the City.' Trans. from the Turkish by V. L. Ménage. Dumbarton Oaks Papers 23/24 (1969-1970): 229-249. doi:10.2307/1291293. Study by a Turkish historian of the Ottoman Empire of Mehmed II's conduct of the assault and sack under Islamic law, his claim to the Roman imperial throne, the repopulation of Istanbul, and the appointment of Gennadios Scholarios as patriarch; draws on Tursun Beg, Kritovoulos, Doukas, Sphrantzes, and Ottoman archival registers. The modern Muslim scholarly lens. Read directly: the legal rule for a city taken by force and the enslavement of its people (p. 232), the sack, its ending on the first evening (citing Runciman), the 'looted and enslaved city', Tursun Beg's 'my throne is Istanbul', and the Roman imperial claim (p. 233), Kritovoulos on the settlement of the enslaved Greeks (p. 235), and the patriarch's appointment (pp. 236-237).
sources.license: Made freely available by Dumbarton Oaks through the Internet Archive; cited for reference. Relevant passages read directly.

sources.citation: Runciman, Steven. The Fall of Constantinople, 1453. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1965. The classic narrative history of the siege, its background in the late Byzantine state and the Florentine union, and its aftermath, presenting the fall as the end of the Christian Roman empire; the academic-history lens. Verified via the Cambridge University Press catalogue and contemporary reviews (Journal of Ecclesiastical History, Slavic Review, Renaissance Quarterly). Relevant passages not read line-by-line.

sources.citation: Philippides, Marios, and Walter K. Hanak. The Siege and the Fall of Constantinople in 1453: Historiography, Topography, and Military Studies. Farnham: Ashgate, 2011. Detailed critical study of the Greek, Latin, Slavonic, and Ottoman sources for the siege and of its topography and military history; the academic-history lens on the sources themselves. Verified via library catalogues and reviews (Bryn Mawr Classical Review 2012.03.27; Reviews in History no. 1101). Relevant passages not read line-by-line.

Verified via Yale University Press and library records. Relevant passages not read line-by-line.

sources.citation: al-Hakim al-Naysaburi, Abu 'Abd Allah (d. 405/1014). al-Mustadrak 'ala al-Sahihayn, with al-Dhahabi's Talkhis, ed. 'Adil Murshid et al. Beirut: Mu'assasat al-Risala. Kitab al-fitan wa-l-malahim, no. 8505 (numbered 8402 and 8300 in other editions): the report through 'Abd Allah ibn Bishr al-Ghanawi from his father, with al-Hakim's judgment 'hadha hadith sahih al-isnad wa-lam yukharrijahu' (a sound chain, not recorded by al-Bukhari and Muslim), al-Dhahabi's notation 'sahih', and the editors' note that all the narrators are trustworthy except 'Abd Allah ibn Bishr, whose name, father's name, and lineage are disputed and therefore also his reliability. The traditionist primary-text lens on the report's grading. Read in an online transcription of the Risala edition, not in the printed volume.
